idiom_name: RustCrypto AEAD crates (aes-gcm) + getrandom for OS entropy
implementation_notes: The standard library deliberately ships no cryptography; the ecosystem's reviewed crates are the mechanism - RustCrypto's algorithms (aes-gcm is "a pure Rust implementation of the AES-GCM AEAD cipher" that "has received one security audit by NCC Group, with no significant findings") and, for keys and nonces, getrandom, which retrieves "high-quality, cryptographically secure random data" from OS sources. What replaces the classic structure: a typed, constant-time AEAD API (Aes256Gcm, Nonce::generate()) where misuse is hard to write, and OS entropy rather than a PRNG; the secret is a key the program must keep out of Debug output and wipe if it leaves the crate's protection. Rust's memory safety removes implementation bug classes but says nothing about protocol design, so "safe" Rust plus a homegrown scheme is still the inversion.
pitfalls: Nonce reuse: the crate documents that the nonce "MUST be unique per message"; generating one with a custom PRNG or a global counter that resets on restart silently destroys GCM's security.
Key material printed or logged: key types may Debug-format their bytes; use secrecy/zeroize wrappers or keep raw bytes out of structured logging.
Assuming memory safety equals a sound protocol: manual composition of primitives, a fixed nonce or a homegrown KDF is unreviewed design even when it is safe Rust.

Portable constant-time claims: aes-gcm's own security notes say the portable backend is constant-time only on processors with constant-time multiplication, so backend/target choice is part of the review.
